svg.title: The five MEF attributes of Carrier Ethernet and what each one changes in a design
svg.desc: Five rows, one per MEF attribute: standardised services, scalability, reliability, quality of service, and service management. Each row names the attribute, states what it means and states the concrete design action it forces, such as demanding the protection switching time or verifying that the CoS mapping matches at both ends. A red note at the bottom says the fifth attribute is the real line between a carrier service and bare fibre or bare Internet, because without OAM and SLA measurement a broken promise cannot be proved.
svg.text: Five attributes that separate a Carrier Ethernet service from a fast pipe
Column three is the only column a design can act on: the attribute, the promise, the question you must ask
ATTRIBUTE
WHAT IT MEANS
WHAT THE DESIGN MUST DO WITH IT
Standardised services
E-Line · E-LAN · E-Tree
Three named service types, so quotes from
two carriers can be compared line by line
Make the quote state the service type and the
topology. "Ethernet" alone is not a service
Scalability
1M to 10G+, many sites
Bandwidth range and site count grow
without redesigning the service
Ask for the per-EVC and per-site ceilings now,
not at the moment you need site forty
Reliability
SLA with protection
Service level commitments including
protection switching on failure
Demand the switching time in milliseconds.
"Protected" without a number is marketing
Quality of service
Multiple CoS per frame
Several classes of service, each markable
per frame, on one circuit
Voice and bulk transfer share one circuit —
only if both ends use the same CoS mapping
Service management
OAM, latency, jitter, loss
The carrier can measure and prove the
service it sold you
Write the measurement points and the reporting
interval into the contract, not into a wish list
Attribute five is the real boundary. Bare fibre and bare Internet fail here: the bits arrive, but nobody can prove where or when they were lost.
Everything else in this list is a capability; attribute five is the evidence that the capability was delivered.
